title: More than a group of houses
goal: Use observations to explain what makes people a community.
setting: Bayani visits a fictional early Philippine community. This illustration helps us think; it is not a record of one actual village.

clues.title: Shared work
clues.text: In the lesson scene, people help repair a shelter together.

clues.title: Responsibilities
clues.text: Different people take care of food, tools and other daily needs.

clues.title: Relationships
clues.text: Families and neighbours depend on one another.

question: Which conclusion do these clues support?
claims: These people share relationships and responsibilities.
Every early community had exactly the same customs.
The houses tell us every rule the community followed.
explanation: Shared work, responsibilities and relationships support the idea of a community. This fictional example cannot prove that every community lived alike.

compare.label: People helping one another
compare.reason: Cooperation can matter in communities in both periods. Its forms vary.

compare.label: The buildings in these two teaching scenes
compare.reason: The drawings show different building materials and designs. They do not represent every home in either period.

claim: The people in this lesson form a community.
limit: We still need other evidence to describe a particular real community.

source.title: Source for this activity: Life in the Barangay

title: How did goods connect people?
goal: Connect exchange to different resources and distinguish a clue from an unsupported claim.
setting: Imagine two communities exchanging useful products. The lesson model explains exchange; archaeological finds provide evidence for real historical contact.

clues.title: Different resources
clues.text: In our model, one community has fish while another has farm products.

clues.title: Exchange
clues.text: The people exchange products to obtain things they need.

clues.title: Archaeological contact
clues.text: Imported ceramics found in Philippine sites provide clues to contact with other Asian places.

question: What is the most careful explanation?
claims: All communities produced exactly the same things.
Exchange could help communities obtain products from elsewhere.
One ceramic bowl records every journey and every trader.
explanation: Different resources can make exchange useful. Imported ceramics support questions about contact, but a single object cannot identify every person or journey.

compare.label: Exchanging goods made in different places
compare.reason: Both teaching scenes show products moving between people and places.

compare.label: The transport shown beside the market
compare.reason: The examples show a small wooden boat and a modern powered vessel. Many types of transport coexist today.

claim: Exchange can connect people with different products.
limit: One find cannot describe an entire trading network.

source.title: National Museum: evidence of maritime relations

title: What can a boat part tell us?
goal: Use material evidence to explain boatbuilding while recognising its limits.
setting: Researchers study wooden boat remains from Butuan. Our drawings are teaching models, not photographs or exact reconstructions of the finds.

clues.title: Wooden planks
clues.text: Recovered wooden parts provide evidence about boat construction.

clues.title: Ways of joining
clues.text: Researchers examine how parts fit together to investigate building techniques.

clues.title: Recorded setting
clues.text: Recording where a part was found helps researchers interpret the evidence.

question: Which claim can the boat remains help us investigate?
claims: The exact name of every passenger.
A complete list of every voyage.
The techniques people used to build wooden boats.
explanation: Wooden parts and their joins provide material evidence about construction. They do not, by themselves, record all passengers or voyages.

compare.label: Using a water route to connect places
compare.reason: Water routes can connect places in both examples.

compare.label: The boat design and propulsion in these examples
compare.reason: The scenes compare a wooden teaching-model boat with a modern powered vessel. Wooden boats are also used today.

claim: Boat remains can help us investigate boatbuilding techniques.
limit: These parts do not identify every person who travelled aboard.

source.title: National Museum: evidence of maritime relations
